strengths: Extensive and carefully controlled experiments spanning multiple model families (Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen-2.5 7B-72B), multiple data sources (Goodfire SAE, Llama Scope SAE, Gemma Scope SAE, Wikipedia contrastive vectors), and multiple adapter architectures, with substantial appendix material supporting the main claims (training curves, PCA analysis, ablations, cross-family replication).

The core finding that a scalar affine adapter (d+1 parameters) captures ~85% of the benefit, and that this simple adapter generalizes better across datasets than higher-capacity alternatives, is a clean and useful empirical insight with a plausible mechanistic explanation (intrinsic dimensionality), supported by targeted controlled experiments (Appendix D) that rule out an alternative explanation (label count).

The application to decoding bridge entities in implicit multi-hop reasoning is a compelling and practically relevant use case, framed sensibly around alignment-auditing motivations, and shows a sizeable, well-quantified improvement over untrained self-interpretation.

The scaling analysis using a 'Taboo' baseline to separate self-interpretation gains from raw model capability gains is a thoughtful experimental design choice that strengthens the scaling claim beyond a naive 'bigger models are better at everything' story.

Reasonably transparent reporting of compute, hyperparameters, and dataset construction (including LLM prompts used for synthetic labeling), aiding reproducibility; code and adapters are stated to be released.

The ALL-CAPS and zero-vector probing experiments (Appendices I, J) provide a nice mechanistic decomposition of what the bias vector versus the input vector contribute, adding interpretability to the interpretability method itself.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is fairly simple (supervised regression/fine-tuning of a small affine map on frozen-model activation injection); most of the paper's value lies in the empirical characterization rather than a methodological advance, and no direct empirical comparison is made against the concurrent LoRA-based self-explanation approaches (LatentQA, Li et al. 2025, Karvonen et al. 2025) that are extensively discussed in related work.

Evaluation relies heavily on proxy metrics (generation scoring via latent activation on self-generated text, and embedding-based retrieval recall) rather than human judgment of interpretability quality or faithfulness; these metrics could reward fluent, plausible-sounding but ungrounded text if correlated with superficial lexical cues, and no human evaluation is reported.

The bridge-entity decoding results, while promising, are not fully ruled out as reflecting learned output-token priors/frequency biases rather than genuine extraction of latent semantic content from the residual stream; the paper acknowledges the adapter has a strong 'default interpretation prior' (bias vector) which raises the question of how much of the entity detection is prompt-consistent guessing versus genuine decoding of internal state.

The claim that 'self-interpretation improves with scale, outpacing capability gains' rests on a single family (Qwen) at only four scales and a single embedding-retrieval metric; the Taboo baseline, while a reasonable control, is itself confounded by task difficulty differences (paraphrase avoidance vs. direct naming) that may not cleanly isolate the intended capability-vs-interpretation distinction.

The explanation for why full-rank adapters overfit on SAE data but not on Wikipedia data (intrinsic dimensionality) is supported only by correlational PCA evidence and two controlled experiments, not a fully causal or theoretical account; alternative explanations (e.g., differences in training objective landscape, dataset size relative to feature diversity) are not fully excluded.

Some claims are stated with strong rhetorical force (e.g., 'trained adapters generate SAE feature labels that outperform the training labels themselves') that, while numerically supported by the specific hit-rate/coverage metrics used, may overstate generality given the narrowness of the evaluation protocol (generation scoring using the same underlying LM that also generated the labels being judged, raising potential for shared biases between generator and evaluator).

strengths: Extensive and carefully controlled empirical study spanning three model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen), scales from 7B to 72B, and three distinct data sources (Goodfire SAEs, Llama/Gemma Scope SAEs, and a newly constructed Wikipedia contrastive-vector dataset), lending good external validity to the central claims.

The core finding that a minimal scalar affine adapter (d+1 parameters) captures ~85% of the achievable improvement, while full-rank adapters catastrophically overfit on SAE data but not on low-intrinsic-dimensionality Wikipedia vectors, is a genuinely interesting and well-supported mechanistic insight, backed by PCA analysis and controlled experiments isolating intrinsic dimensionality from label-count confounds (Appendix D).

The 'Taboo' baseline is a thoughtful control that isolates self-interpretation gains from raw capability gains across scale, strengthening the claim that self-interpretation quality scales favorably and non-trivially with model size.

The multi-hop reasoning / bridge-entity experiment is a compelling and novel application, showing the method generalizes from monosemantic training vectors to polysemantic residual-stream activations, with a large and clearly quantified improvement over untrained SelfIE.

Very strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, prompts, dataset construction pipeline, and compute accounting are all provided, and results are validated with SEMs and significance tests in the main tables.

The zero-vector and ALL-CAPS probing experiments (Appendices I, J) provide genuinely useful mechanistic insight into what the bias vector versus the input vector each contribute, going beyond a pure benchmark paper.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against the decoder-finetuning alternatives (LatentQA, Li et al. 2025, Karvonen et al. 2025) that are discussed extensively as 'concurrent work'; the central positioning claim (frozen adapters vs. fine-tuning trade-off) is argued conceptually but not tested head-to-head on a shared task/dataset.

The generation-scoring and embedding-retrieval metrics are indirect proxies for interpretability quality (reactivation of a latent, or nearest-neighbor match in embedding space) rather than direct human judgments of description correctness; no human evaluation is included to corroborate the qualitative examples.

The best-of-6 protocol, while applied equally to baselines, still relies on a calibration step to select the scale grid per dataset/method, which could partially inflate reported gains and makes exact reproduction of the 'multi-scale' numbers somewhat dependent on this calibration procedure.

Because scalar affine adapters only apply a uniform scale and additive bias while preserving direction, and the bias vector accounts for the large majority of the improvement, it is unclear how much genuine per-vector (i.e., direction-specific) information is actually being read out versus how much of the gain reflects the adapter learning a better generic prior/target distribution for the self-interpretation task.

The Wikipedia contrastive-vector dataset (both training labels and part of the evaluation pipeline) is constructed and filtered using an LLM (Claude), and evaluated via another off-the-shelf embedding model; this introduces potential circularity/leakage concerns between data construction and evaluation that are not fully addressed.

The scaling analysis (Section 3.3) rests on only four model sizes within one model family (Qwen-2.5), and the appendix shows a non-monotonic trend at the single-layer level (32B underperforming 14B), suggesting the 'scaling law' claim is somewhat sensitive to methodological choices (layer pooling vs. single-layer evaluation).

The paper's framing of adapters 'outperforming training labels themselves' is an interesting result but is somewhat expected for any model that aggregates structure across thousands of noisy labels (akin to denoising by regression); the framing could be tempered or more precisely contextualized relative to this expectation.
